chapter.title: Nietzsche and the modern turn: who decides what is true or good

cards.body: For about 2,300 years the guests at the table argued over what is true and what is good. In the 1880s Friedrich Nietzsche sits down and does not answer the last speaker. He asks who wrote the menu, and what they got out of it. That is the fourth of the 4 questions: who gets to decide.

cards.title: Values have a history
cards.body:
Nietzsche's starting point is simple. Words like "good", "evil" and "guilt" were not handed down from the sky. People made them, at a time, for a reason. He called the study of where a value came from a "genealogy", which just means a family tree.

That is a shift. Mill asked "does it make people happy?" Kant asked "could everyone act this way?" Both treat a value as a claim to test. Nietzsche asks a different thing: who first said this, and what did saying it do for them?

Behind that sits a harder claim. In 1882 he wrote "God is dead." He was not reporting an event. He meant the shared ground under European values, the belief that God fixed what is good, had crumbled, and most people had not noticed they were now standing on nothing.

A line from his notebooks puts it sharply: "there are no facts, only interpretations." He means there is no view from nowhere. Every claim of truth is said by someone, standing somewhere, wanting something.

So his question is not "is this true?" but "who made this, and who gains from it?"

cards.prompt: Nietzsche hears someone say "humility is a virtue." Which question is he most likely to ask?

options.text: But is humility really good for everyone to practise?
Who first called humility good, and what did they gain by it?
How could we ever know that humility is good?

whyNot.a: That's Kant's test, not Nietzsche's question: Kant asks whether the rule holds for everyone, Nietzsche asks where the rule came from.
whyNot.c: That's the "how would we know" question from Descartes and Hume, not Nietzsche's: he asks about a value's history, not our evidence for it.

cards.reteach: Nietzsche treats a value like a family heirloom. He does not ask whether the heirloom is beautiful. He asks who first owned it, who passed it on, and what they got for doing so.

cards.title: The word "good" flips
cards.body: In On the Genealogy of Morality, published in 1887, Nietzsche told a story about the word "good." At first, he said, the strong and noble used "good" to describe themselves: bold, proud, powerful. "Bad" just meant common or low. Then, he argued, the powerless turned the table over: meek, patient and humble became "good", and the proud and strong became "evil." He called this the "slave revolt in morality" and tied it to priests and to early Christianity. Historians dispute his story, but notice the shape of the move. He never argues that humility is bad. He argues that calling it good was done by someone, for a reason.

cards.title: Who pushes back
cards.body:
Nietzsche was taking an old seat. In the 400s BC Protagoras said "man is the measure of all things", meaning what is true for you is true for you. Plato wrote a whole dialogue against him, and his sharpest reply is still in use: if every view is only an opinion, then "every view is only an opinion" is also only an opinion. Why should anyone accept it?

Kant pushes back from the other side. Even if a value has a history, reason can still test it. The rule "could everyone act this way" does not care who first wrote it down.

Nietzsche's method outlived him. In the 1970s Michel Foucault borrowed the word "genealogy" to ask how prisons and schools came to decide who counts as normal. Today, when someone says "history is written by the winners" or "that is just your opinion", they are sitting in the seat Protagoras and Nietzsche kept warm. Plato is across the table, waiting.

cards.prompt: A friend says: "There's no real truth about the past. History is just whatever the winners wrote." Place it in the long argument.

options.text: It echoes Nietzsche's "who decides" question. Plato pushes back: is "there's no real truth" itself true?
It echoes Descartes doubting everything. Hume pushes back that all knowledge comes through the senses.
It echoes Kant's "could everyone act this way" test. Mill pushes back with the happiness test.

whyNot.b: That's the "how would we know" line, not "who decides": Descartes doubted to find sure footing, your friend says the footing was built by whoever had power.
whyNot.c: That's the "is it right" debate between Kant and Mill, not the question of who gets to decide what counts as true.

cards.reteach: Your friend is not asking whether a history book is accurate. They are asking who wrote it and what they gained. That is Nietzsche's question, with Protagoras behind him. The standard reply is Plato's: a claim that nothing is true has to include itself.

cards.body: The common slip is to think that showing where a belief came from proves it false. "You only believe hard work is good because your parents drilled it into you" may be true, and hard work may still be good. Philosophers call this the genetic fallacy, which means judging an idea by its origin instead of its reasons. Spot it when a sentence starts "you only think that because..." and never gets round to whether the thing is true.

cards.prompt: What was the new question Nietzsche brought to the table?

options.text: Does this value produce the most happiness?
Where did this value come from, and who gained from it?
Can I doubt this value, and what is left when I do?

whyNot.a: That's Mill's test, not Nietzsche's question: Mill counted outcomes, Nietzsche traced origins.
whyNot.c: That's Descartes' method, not Nietzsche's: Descartes looked for something certain, Nietzsche looked for a history.

cards.reteach: The other guests tested values. Nietzsche traced them. His question is a family tree, not a verdict: who made this, when, and what did it do for them.

cards.body: Tonight, write down one value you hold, like "hard work is good." Under it, write where you got it and who gained from you believing it. Then ask Plato's question: does that history make it false?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now hear "that's just your opinion", place it in the seat Protagoras and Nietzsche took, and give Plato's one-line reply.
